preamble: The palatalized voiced stop [dʲ] becomes the voiced alveolo-palatal fricative [ʑ]. The change is not a single step: [dʲ] first affricates to [dʑ], and the affricate then loses its stop closure (deaffrication). Lower Sorbian shows the full chain: West Slavic soft *dʲ became dź [dʑ], as it still is in Polish and Upper Sorbian, and Lower Sorbian then reduced dź to ź [ʑ], so Upper Sorbian dźeń 'day' corresponds to Lower Sorbian źeń. Japanese took a parallel route before [i]: Old Japanese /di/ was affricated to [dʑi] and then merged with /zi/, realized as fricative [ʑi] especially between vowels.

examples.note: Soft *dʲ first became the affricate dź (kept in Upper Sorbian dźeń and Polish dzień), and Lower Sorbian then lost the stop closure. This happened in the western dialects around the mid-16th century and about a century later in the east.
Upper Sorbian keeps the affricate (dźiwi). Lower Sorbian keeps dź after a dental fricative, as in pozdźej 'later', so the change is blocked in that position.

examples.period: Late Middle Japanese to Early Modern Japanese
examples.note: /di/ (ぢ) became [dʑi] and merged with /zi/ (じ) in the yotsugana merger. The merged sound is [(d)ʑi], with the fricative [ʑ] usual between vowels in Standard Japanese.
